x: Parliamentary government came from Britain, DPSP from Ireland, a federation with a strong Centre from Canada and the Concurrent List from Australia. Option A wrongly gives the parliamentary form to Ireland.
t: Recall the signature borrowing of each country.

x: C is incorrect: the amendment procedure was borrowed from South Africa, not Ireland (Ireland gave DPSP). Procedure established by law is from Japan, the Republic from France, and Emergency provisions (except financial) from Germany's Weimar Constitution.
t: Check the country against each borrowed feature.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: Fundamental Duties and the ideals of social, economic and political justice were two separate borrowings from the USSR.
t: Two borrowings from one country do not explain each other.

x: I, II and III are correct: judicial review, the Vice-President and removal of judges came from the USA. IV is wrong: the idea of the Preamble is also from the USA; France gave liberty, equality, fraternity and the Republic.
t: Separate the idea of the Preamble (USA) from its ideals (France).

x: Both are true: the Government of India Act, 1935 gave the structural and administrative backbone, and the language of the Preamble came from Australia.
t: Recall the 1935 Act as the main blueprint.

x: The Cabinet system was borrowed from Britain, along with parliamentary government and the Rule of Law. Canada gave federalism with a strong Centre; Ireland gave DPSP.
t: Link the Cabinet system to the Westminster model.

x: Single citizenship came from Britain, impeachment of the President from the USA, the method of electing the President from Ireland and the joint sitting of both Houses from Australia.
t: Link each provision to its source country one by one.
s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Single citizenship
(b) Impeachment of the President
(c) Method of election of the President
(d) Joint sitting of both Houses

List-II
(i) Britain
(ii) USA
(iii) Ireland
(iv) Australia

x: All three came from the USA: Fundamental Rights, independence of the judiciary and impeachment of the President.
t: Recall the US borrowings on rights and the judiciary.
s:
Consider the following statements:

I. Fundamental Rights were borrowed from the USA.
II. The independence of the judiciary was borrowed from the USA.
III. The impeachment of the President was borrowed from the USA.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: Both are true: Ireland gave the method of election of the President and the nomination of members to the Rajya Sabha (along with DPSP).
t: Recall Ireland's three borrowings.

x: Residuary powers with the Centre came from Canada, the Rule of Law from Britain, nomination of members to the Rajya Sabha from Ireland and freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse from Australia.
t: Recall each borrowed feature's source country.
s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Residuary powers with the Centre
(b) Rule of Law
(c) Nomination of members to the Rajya Sabha
(d) Freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse

List-II
(i) Canada
(ii) Britain
(iii) Ireland
(iv) Australia

x: Three: joint sitting, freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse and the language of the Preamble came from Australia. DPSP came from Ireland.
t: Remove the item that belongs to Ireland and count.

x: Election of Rajya Sabha members was borrowed from South Africa, along with the amendment procedure. Nomination of members to the Rajya Sabha came from Ireland — the trap.
t: Distinguish election (South Africa) from nomination (Ireland).

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: liberty, equality and fraternity and the ideal of a Republic were separate borrowings from France.
t: Two borrowings from France are independent.

x: The federal scheme came from the Government of India Act, 1935, judicial review from the USA, DPSP from Ireland, residuary powers with the Centre from Canada and the Republic from France.
t: Separate the 1935 Act's structural features from foreign borrowings.
s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Federal scheme
(b) Judicial review
(c) Directive Principles of State Policy
(d) Residuary powers with the Centre
(e) Ideal of a Republic

List-II
(i) Government of India Act, 1935
(ii) USA
(iii) Ireland
(iv) Canada
(v) France

x: Article 1 says India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States. Article 2 is admission of new States, Article 3 alteration of boundaries, and Article 11 Parliament's power over citizenship.
t: Match the opening Article to the nature of the Union.

x: B is incorrect: Article 4 says laws under Articles 2 and 3 are NOT amendments under Article 368 — they pass by simple majority. The others are right: Article 2 new States, Article 3 boundaries, Articles 5–11 citizenship.
t: Watch for a dropped 'not'.

x: Both are true and R explains A: Article 13 makes laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights void, which is the basis for courts to review and strike them down.
t: Ask whether R is the mechanism behind A.

x: Both are true: Article 14 provides equality before law and Article 17 abolishes untouchability.
t: Recall the Article numbers of the equality rights.

x: All three are correct: Article 37 makes DPSP non-justiciable but fundamental in governance, Article 43A covers workers' participation in management, and Article 50 separates the judiciary from the executive.
t: Check each DPSP Article against its subject.

x: Equal justice and free legal aid – Article 39A; humane conditions of work – Article 42; Uniform Civil Code – Article 44; environment – Article 48A.
t: Fix one Article you know (44 = UCC), then match the rest.

x: Three: Articles 14, 21 and 32 are Fundamental Rights (Part III). Article 40 (village panchayats) is a Directive Principle in Part IV.
t: Fundamental Rights lie in Articles 12–35.

x: Article 21A (added by the 86th Amendment, 2002) makes education a Fundamental Right for children aged 6–14. Article 45 now covers early childhood care; Article 21 is life and liberty.
t: Distinguish 21 from 21A and from DPSP Article 45.

x: Article 52 – there shall be a President; Article 54 – election; Article 60 – oath; Article 61 – impeachment.
t: Follow the sequence of President Articles from 52 onwards.

x: Both are true and R explains A: Article 64 is the provision that makes the Vice-President ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.
t: Check whether R is the source of the role in A.

x: All three are correct: Article 93 – Speaker and Deputy Speaker; Article 108 – joint sitting; Article 112 – Annual Financial Statement (Budget).
t: Recall the Parliament Articles by number.

x: Article 110 defines a Money Bill; Article 109 lays down the special procedure for it. Article 108 is joint sitting, 111 assent to Bills and 117 Financial Bills.
t: Recall the Article that defines a Money Bill.
s: Which Article of the Constitution defines a Money Bill?

x: Supreme Court established – Article 124; review of judgments – Article 137; High Court writs – Article 226; High Court superintendence – Article 227.
t: Pair the two High Court powers: 226 writs, 227 superintendence.

x: Both are true: Article 248 gives residuary powers to Parliament and Article 249 lets it legislate on a State subject in the national interest (on a Rajya Sabha resolution).
t: Recall the two consecutive Articles on Parliament's powers.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: Article 357 only says how legislative power is exercised once President's Rule is in force; it does not explain Article 356 itself.
t: A follow-up provision does not explain the main one.

x: Finance Commission – Article 280; Election Commission – Article 324; National Commission for SCs – Article 338; Backward Classes Commission – Article 340.
t: Match each commission to its Article.

x: Articles 243 to 243O (Part IX, 73rd Amendment) deal with Panchayats. 243P to 243ZG cover Municipalities (74th Amendment) and 301–307 trade and commerce.
t: Separate the Panchayat range from the Municipality range.

x: Article 12 defines 'State'; Article 15 prohibits discrimination; Article 16 gives equality of opportunity in public employment; Article 18 abolishes titles.
t: Recall the order of Articles 12–18.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: A states what Article 15(4) allows (special provisions), while R only gives its history (added by the First Amendment, 1951).
t: History of a clause does not explain its content.

x: Article 20 protects in respect of conviction; Article 22 against arrest and detention; Article 23 prohibits traffic in human beings and forced labour; Article 24 prohibits employment of children in factories.
t: Recall the Article numbers of Articles 20 to 24 in order.
s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Article 20
(b) Article 22
(c) Article 23
(d) Article 24

List-II
(i) Prohibition of traffic in human beings and forced labour
(ii) Protection in respect of conviction for offences
(iii) Protection against arrest and detention
(iv) Prohibition of employment of children in factories

x: Article 21A – Right to Education (86th Amendment); Articles 25–28 – freedom of religion; Articles 29–30 – minorities' cultural and educational rights; Article 32 – constitutional remedies, Ambedkar's 'heart and soul'.
t: Match each block of Articles to its right.

x: Both are true: Articles 33–35 let Parliament modify Fundamental Rights for the forces and similar groups, and Article 36 defines 'State' for Part IV (as Article 12 does for Part III).
t: Recall that 'State' is defined twice: Article 12 and Article 36.

x: All four are correct: Article 38 – social order and welfare; Article 39 – livelihood and, in 39(d), equal pay; Article 39A – added by the 42nd Amendment.
t: Check each DPSP Article and the amendment that added 39A.
s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Article 38 concerns social order and welfare.
II. Article 39(d) concerns equal pay.
III. Article 39 concerns livelihood.
IV. Article 39A was inserted by the 42nd Amendment.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: Article 41 covers the right to work, to education and to public assistance. Article 40 is village panchayats, 39 the principles of policy and 42 humane conditions of work.
t: Separate the right to work (41) from conditions of work (42).

x: Article 36 – definition of 'State'; Article 43 – living wage; Article 49 – protection of monuments; Article 51 – international peace.
t: Match each DPSP Article to its subject.

x: All four are correct: Articles 39A, 43A and 48A were added by the 42nd Amendment (1976), and Article 45, once free education up to 14, now covers early childhood care after the 86th Amendment.
t: Remember the three Articles with 'A' added in 1976.
s:
Consider the following statements:

I. Article 43A was inserted by the 42nd Amendment.
II. Article 48A was inserted by the 42nd Amendment.
III. Article 39A was inserted by the 42nd Amendment.
IV. Article 45 originally concerned free education until the age of 14 and now concerns early childhood care.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: Both are true and R explains A: Article 46 asks the State to promote the educational and economic interests of SCs and STs — R simply spells out the two parts of A.
t: Check whether R restates the content of A.

x: Article 40 directs the State to organise village panchayats. Articles 39, 41 and 43 cover principles of policy, right to work and living wage.
t: Link Article 40 with village panchayats.

x: All three are correct: Article 41 covers the right to work, to education and to public assistance in old age, sickness and unemployment.
t: Recall the three parts of Article 41.
s:
Consider the following statements:

I. Article 41 concerns the right to work.
II. Article 41 concerns the right to education.
III. Article 41 concerns public assistance.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: Article 47 covers nutrition levels and prohibition of intoxicating drinks; Article 48 covers organisation of agriculture and animal husbandry (including cow protection).
t: Split health items (47) from agriculture items (48).

x: I and III are correct: Article 51A has 11 Fundamental Duties and the 86th Amendment (2002) added the eleventh. II is wrong: the 42nd Amendment (1976) added only ten duties.
t: Count how many duties each Amendment added.
s:
Consider the following statements:

I. Article 51A contains 11 Fundamental Duties.
II. All 11 Fundamental Duties under Article 51A were added by the 42nd Amendment.
III. The 11th Fundamental Duty under Article 51A was added by the 86th Amendment.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: Article 53 vests the Union's executive power in the President. The Council of Ministers (Article 74) only aids and advises.
t: Distinguish where power is vested from who advises.

x: Article 55 – manner of election; Article 56 – term of office; Article 57 – re-election; Article 58 – qualifications.
t: Follow the order 55 to 58 for the President.

x: All four are correct: Article 63 – there shall be a Vice-President; 65 – acting as President; 66 – election; 67 – term and removal.
t: Recall the Vice-President Articles 63–67.
s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Article 63 provides that there shall be a Vice-President.
II. Article 65 provides for the Vice-President to act as President.
III. Article 66 concerns the election of the Vice-President.
IV. Article 67 concerns the term and removal of the Vice-President.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: Article 74 – Council of Ministers to aid and advise; Article 75(3) – collective responsibility to the Lok Sabha; Article 75(1A) – 15% size limit; Article 76 – Attorney-General.
t: Separate the two clauses of Article 75.

x: All three are correct: Article 75 contains other provisions on Ministers, its clause (1A) was added by the 91st Amendment (2003), and Article 77 covers the conduct of business of the Government of India.
t: Link 75(1A) to the 91st Amendment.
s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Article 75 concerns other provisions regarding Ministers.
II. Article 75(1A) was inserted by the 91st Amendment.
III. Article 77 concerns the conduct of the business of the Government of India.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: Article 79 – constitution of Parliament; Article 80 – composition of the Rajya Sabha; Article 81 – composition of the Lok Sabha; Article 83 – duration of the Houses. The Council of States (80) comes before the House of the People (81).
t: Remember the Rajya Sabha Article precedes the Lok Sabha one.

x: Both are true but unrelated: Article 85 covers sessions, prorogation and dissolution, while Article 87 covers the President's special address — neither explains the other.
t: Two neighbouring Articles on different subjects.

x: All four are correct: Article 100 – voting and quorum; 105 – powers and privileges of Parliament; 113 – procedure for estimates; 114 – Appropriation Bills.
t: Check each Article against its parliamentary procedure.
s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Article 100 concerns voting and quorum.
II. Article 105 concerns the powers and privileges of the Houses of Parliament.
III. Article 113 concerns the procedure for estimates.
IV. Article 114 concerns Appropriation Bills.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: Article 116 covers both votes on account and votes of credit (so two rows map to it); Article 123 gives the President's ordinance power; Article 125 fixes Supreme Court judges' salaries.
t: Expect two rows to share Article 116.

x: Article 127 – ad hoc Judges; Article 129 – Supreme Court as a Court of Record; Article 131 – original jurisdiction; Articles 132–136 – appellate jurisdiction.
t: Match the single Articles first, leaving the range for appeals.

x: Article 141 – law declared by the Supreme Court binds all courts; Article 143 – advisory jurisdiction on a Presidential reference; Articles 148–151 – CAG; Article 214 – High Courts for States.
t: Separate binding law (141) from advisory opinion (143).

x: Article 215 – High Courts as Courts of Record; 216 – constitution of High Courts; 217 – appointment and service of High Court Judges; 233 – appointment of District Judges.
t: Mirror the Supreme Court pattern: Court of Record before constitution.

x: All four are correct: Articles 245–255 deal with legislative relations; 246 with the three Lists; 250 with State subjects during an Emergency; 252 with laws by consent of States; and 253 with laws to implement international agreements.
t: Check each special case of Parliament legislating on State subjects.
s:
Consider the following statements:

I. Articles 245 to 255 concern legislative relations.
II. Article 246 concerns the subject matter of laws under the Union, State and Concurrent Lists.
III. Article 250 concerns legislation on the State List during an Emergency, while Article 252 concerns legislation by consent of States.
IV. Article 253 concerns legislation for international agreements.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: Both are true: Articles 256–263 are on administrative relations, ending with Article 263 on the Inter-State Council.
t: Recall the range and its last Article.

x: Both are true: Articles 268–281 deal with distribution of revenues, ending with Article 281 on the Finance Commission's recommendations (the Commission itself is Article 280).
t: Separate Article 280 (Commission) from 281 (recommendations).

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: Article 353 states the effects of a proclamation; it does not explain Article 352, which provides for the proclamation itself.
t: An Article on effects does not explain the Article on the proclamation.

x: Article 354 – revenue distribution during Emergency; 355 – Union's duty to protect States; 358 – suspension of Article 19; 359 – suspension of enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
t: Separate the automatic suspension of Article 19 (358) from enforcement (359).

x: Article 360 provides for a Financial Emergency. Article 352 is National Emergency, 356 President's Rule and 358 the suspension of Article 19.
t: Recall the three Emergency Articles: 352, 356, 360.

x: Article 312 empowers Parliament to create All-India Services. Public Service Commissions are Articles 315–323, the Election Commission Article 324 and Official Language Articles 343–351.
t: Link Article 312 to All-India Services.

x: Articles 315–323 – Public Service Commissions; Article 326 – adult suffrage; Articles 330–334 – reservation of seats for SCs, STs and Anglo-Indians; Articles 343–351 – Official Language.
t: Match each Article range to its subject.

x: Both are true: Article 368 gives Parliament the power to amend the Constitution, and Articles 371 to 371J make special provisions for certain States.
t: Recall Article 368 and the 371 series.

x: Both are true: Article 16(4) allows reservation for backward classes in appointments and 16(4A) allows reservation in promotions for SCs and STs.
t: Distinguish appointments (16(4)) from promotions (16(4A)).

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: Article 370 gave temporary provisions for Jammu and Kashmir; being inoperative now (since 2019) is its current status, not the reason for its content.
t: Current status does not explain the original provision.

x: Article 43 – living wage; Article 43A – inserted by the 42nd Amendment (workers' participation); Article 44 – Uniform Civil Code; Article 45 – early childhood care.
t: Fix Article 44 (UCC), then place the rest.

x: All four are correct: Article 48 covers agriculture, animal husbandry and cow protection; Article 49 protects monuments; Article 50 separates the judiciary from the executive.
t: Check each consecutive DPSP Article.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: Article 48A's subject (environment) is not explained by the fact that the 42nd Amendment inserted it.
t: When an Article was added does not explain what it says.

x: Article 19 lists the six freedoms in clauses 19(1)(a) to 19(1)(g). Article 21 is life and liberty, 25–28 freedom of religion and 29–30 minority rights.
t: Link the six freedoms to Article 19.

x: Article 338A – National Commission for STs; 338B – National Commission for Backward Classes; 243ZD – District Planning Committees; 243ZE – Metropolitan Planning Committees.
t: Order alphabetically: A before B, ZD (district) before ZE (metropolitan).

x: C is incorrect: Part XXI (Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions) covers Articles 369 to 392; Articles 393 to 395 form Part XXII. The other Part ranges are right.
t: Check the last Article of each Part.

x: Both are true and R explains A: Part IX deals with Panchayats because the 73rd Amendment (1992) inserted it for that purpose.
t: Ask whether R is how Part IX came to cover Panchayats.

x: Part I – the Union and its Territory; Part II – Citizenship; Part V – the Union (executive, Parliament, judiciary); Part XX – Amendment of the Constitution. Option A swaps Parts II and V.
t: Separate 'the Union and its Territory' (I) from 'the Union' (V).

x: All four are correct: Part III – Fundamental Rights, Articles 12–35; Part XII – Finance, Property, Contracts and Suits, Articles 264–300A; Part XVII – Official Language, 343–351; Part XX – Article 368.
t: Check each Part's subject and range.
s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Part III deals with Fundamental Rights and covers Articles 12 to 35.
II. Part XII deals with Finance, Property, Contracts and Suits and covers Articles 264 to 300-A.
III. Part XVII deals with Official Language and covers Articles 343 to 351.
IV. Part XX contains Article 368 relating to Amendment of the Constitution.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: All three are correct: the Constitution had 22 Parts originally and has 25 now; Parts IVA, IXA, IXB and XIVA were added later (and Part VII was repealed).
t: Remember additions and the one repeal.

x: Part I – Articles 1–4; Part II – Articles 5–11; Part IV (DPSP) – Articles 36–51; Part VIII (Union Territories) – Articles 239–242.
t: Match each Part to its Article range.

x: Both are true and R explains A: Part IVA (Fundamental Duties, Article 51A) counts as 'added later' because the 42nd Amendment inserted it in 1976.
t: Check whether R is the reason the Part is a later addition.

x: Both are true: Parts I (Union and territory), II (Citizenship), III (Fundamental Rights) and IV (DPSP) were all in the original Constitution.
t: Recall which early Parts are original.

x: Part V – the Union, Articles 52–151; Part VI – the States, 152–237; Part VII – Part B States, repealed by the 7th Amendment (1956); Part VIII – Union Territories, 239–242.
t: Remember Part VII is the repealed one.

x: All three are correct: Part IX – Articles 243–243O; Part IXA – Municipalities, 243P–243ZG; Part IXB – Co-operative Societies, 243ZH–243ZT, added by the 97th Amendment (2011).
t: Recall the three Parts on local bodies and co-operatives.

x: Both are true: Part X (Scheduled and Tribal Areas, Articles 244–244A) and Part XI (Union-State relations, Articles 245–263) were both in the original Constitution.
t: Check each Part's subject, range and status.

x: Both are true: Part XII was original, and Part XIII (trade, commerce and intercourse, Articles 301–307) was also original.
t: Recall the original Parts XII and XIII.

x: Part XIV – Services, Articles 308–323; Part XIVA – Tribunals, 323A–323B; Part XV – Elections, 324–329A; Part XVI – special provisions for certain classes.
t: Use the Article ranges in sequence to place each Part.

x: Both are true: Part XIV (Services) was original, while Part XIVA (Tribunals) was added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976.
t: Separate the original Part from its 'A' addition.

x: Part XV (Elections) was in the original Constitution. The 42nd, 73rd and 97th Amendments added Parts IVA/XIVA, IX and IXB respectively.
t: Recall which Parts were added by amendments; the rest are original.

x: Part XVI – special provisions for certain classes (330–342); Part XVII – Official Language (343–351); Part XVIII – Emergency (352–360); Part XIX – Miscellaneous (361–367). All are original.
t: Order by Article range: 330, 343, 352, 361.

x: All three are correct: Parts XX (amendment), XXI (temporary, transitional and special provisions) and XXII (short title, commencement, Hindi text, repeals) were all original.
t: Recall the last three Parts as original.

x: Part IVA – Article 51A; Part V – Articles 52–151; Part XIVA – Articles 323A–323B; Part XX – Article 368.
t: Match each Part to its Article(s).

x: Part IXA (Municipalities) was added by the 74th Amendment, 1992. The 73rd (1992) added Part IX, the 97th (2011) Part IXB and the 42nd (1976) Parts IVA and XIVA.
t: Pair 73rd–IX and 74th–IXA.

x: Part IXB (Articles 243ZH–243ZT) deals with Co-operative Societies. Panchayats are Part IX, Municipalities Part IXA and Tribunals Part XIVA.
t: Recall the subject of the Part added in 2011.

x: The Constitution now has 12 Schedules: it began with 8, and four (9th to 12th) were added by amendments.
t: Add the four later Schedules to the original eight.

x: B is incorrect: the 11th Schedule (Panchayats) was added by the 73rd Amendment; the 12th Schedule (Municipalities) by the 74th, both in 1992. The 9th (1951) and 10th (1985) are stated correctly.
t: Pair 73rd with the 11th Schedule and 74th with the 12th.

x: Both are true and R explains A: the 9th Schedule, added by the 1st Amendment (1951), validates listed Acts — mainly land reforms — which is how it shields them from judicial review.
t: Ask whether R describes the purpose stated in A.

x: 1st Schedule – names and territories of States and UTs; 4th – Rajya Sabha seats; 7th – Union, State and Concurrent Lists; 10th – anti-defection.
t: Match the best-known Schedules first.

x: I, II and IV are correct: the Eighth Schedule grew from 14 to 22 languages; Sindhi came by the 21st Amendment (1967) and Bodo, Dogri, Maithili and Santhali by the 92nd (2003). III is wrong: Konkani, Manipuri and Nepali were added by the 71st Amendment (1992).
t: Pair each batch of languages with its amendment.
s:
Consider the following statements:

I. The Eighth Schedule originally contained 14 languages and presently contains 22 languages.
II. Sindhi was added to the Eighth Schedule by the 21st Amendment in 1967.
III. Konkani, Manipuri and Nepali were added by the 92nd Amendment in 2003.
IV. Bodo, Dogri, Maithili and Santhali were added by the 92nd Amendment in 2003.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: 2nd Schedule – emoluments and privileges of constitutional authorities; 3rd – oaths and affirmations; 5th – Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes; 6th – tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.
t: Separate the 5th (Scheduled Areas) from the 6th (four NE States).

x: All four are correct: the 1st to 4th Schedules were all in the original Constitution, which had eight Schedules.
t: Remember that Schedules 1–8 are original.
s:
Consider the following statements:

I. The First Schedule was part of the original Constitution.
II. The Second Schedule was part of the original Constitution.
III. The Third Schedule was part of the original Constitution.
IV. The Fourth Schedule was part of the original Constitution.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: Both are true: the 5th and 6th Schedules (Scheduled and tribal areas) were part of the original Constitution.
t: Schedules 1 to 8 are all original.

x: The Seventh Schedule, an original Schedule, contains the Union, State and Concurrent Lists. The 4th is Rajya Sabha seats, the 6th tribal areas and the 8th languages.
t: Link the three Lists to the Seventh Schedule.

x: 10th Schedule – disqualification of MPs and MLAs on defection; 11th – Panchayats, 29 subjects; 12th – Municipalities, 18 subjects.
t: Panchayats have more subjects (29) than Municipalities (18).

x: All three are correct: Union List 97 → 100 subjects, State List 66 → 61, Concurrent List 47 → 52 (transfers such as the 42nd Amendment moved items from the State List).
t: Note the State List shrank while the other two grew.
s:
Consider the following statements about the Lists in the Seventh Schedule:

I. The Union List originally contained 97 subjects and now contains 100 subjects.
II. The State List originally contained 66 subjects and now contains 61 subjects.
III. The Concurrent List originally contained 47 subjects and now contains 52 subjects.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: Both are true: the Ninth Schedule began with 13 Acts in 1951 and now has around 284.
t: Recall the starting and present counts.

x: The 91st Amendment (2003) further amended the anti-defection law, deleting the 'split' exception. The law itself came with the 52nd Amendment (1985).
t: Separate the amendment that created the law from the one that tightened it.

x: Article 246 puts subjects into the Union, State and Concurrent Lists. Article 248 is residuary power, 250 Emergency legislation and 254 repugnancy.
t: Link the three-list distribution to Article 246.

x: I, II and III are correct under Article 246: Parliament alone for the Union List, States alone for the State List, both for the Concurrent List. IV is wrong because the Concurrent List is shared, not exclusive to States.
t: 'Concurrent' means shared, never exclusive.
s:
Consider the following statements:
I. State Legislatures have exclusive legislative competence over the State List.
II. Both Parliament and State Legislatures have competence over the Concurrent List.
III. Parliament has exclusive competence over the Union List.
IV. State Legislatures have exclusive competence over the Concurrent List.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: Railways – Union List; Police – State List; Education – moved from the State List to the Concurrent List by the 42nd Amendment (1976); marriage, divorce and adoption – an original Concurrent List entry.
t: Separate original Concurrent entries from those transferred in 1976.
s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Railways
(b) Police
(c) Education
(d) Marriage, Divorce and Adoption

List-II
(i) Union List
(ii) State List
(iii) Concurrent List since 1950
(iv) Moved from the State List to the Concurrent List by the 42nd Amendment

x: Article 248 gives Parliament exclusive residuary power over subjects in no List — as in Canada, unlike the USA and Australia, where States hold it.
t: Remember India follows Canada on residuary powers.

x: B is incorrect: repugnancy on a Concurrent subject is dealt with by Article 254, not 250 (Emergency legislation). Under 254 the Central law prevails unless a State law reserved for the President gets his assent (254(2)).
t: Check the Article number given for repugnancy.

x: All four, along with administration of justice, were the five subjects moved from the State List to the Concurrent List by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.
t: Recall the five subjects shifted in 1976.

x: A law under Article 249 ceases six months after the Rajya Sabha resolution lapses (each resolution lasts one year and can be renewed).
t: Separate the one-year resolution from the six-month grace period.

x: Both are true: under Article 250 Parliament can legislate on State subjects during a National Emergency, and such laws lapse six months after the Emergency ends.
t: Recall the six-month rule after the Emergency.

x: C is incorrect: a law under Article 252 applies only to the States that passed resolutions (and any that adopt it later). It is passed on the request of two or more States and can be amended only by Parliament.
t: Watch for 'automatically applies to every State'.

x: Article 253 lets Parliament make any law, even on State subjects, to implement international treaties and agreements.
t: Link Article 253 to treaty implementation.

x: During President's Rule under Article 356, Parliament exercises the State Legislature's powers. Article 249 needs a Rajya Sabha resolution, 252 States' consent and 253 a treaty.
t: Match the trigger (President's Rule) to Article 356.

x: Two: Economic and social planning and price control are Concurrent subjects. Railway police falls under police (State List) and census is a Union subject.
t: Classify each subject, then count Concurrent ones.

x: A is true (Corporation Tax – Union List; Land Revenue – State List). B is false: economic and social planning is Concurrent List Entry 20.
t: Check the List of each subject.

x: A is true: Article 246A gives both Parliament and State Legislatures power to make GST laws. B is false: Panchayati Raj and Municipalities are State List subjects (Entry 5).
t: Local government is a State subject.

x: Inter-State trade and commerce – Union List Entry 42; public health and sanitation – State List; criminal law and procedure – Concurrent List; Corporation Tax – Union List Entry 85.
t: Place each subject in its List, then match the Union entry numbers.
s:

(b) Public Health and Sanitation

(i) State List
(ii) Concurrent List

x: The Seventh Schedule works with Part XI, Articles 245–255 (legislative relations). Articles 256–263 are administrative relations; Part X is Scheduled Areas.
t: Link the Lists to the legislative-relations Articles.

x: Article 246A, added by the 101st Amendment (2016), is the special provision for GST. Articles 248, 249 and 254 deal with residuary power, national interest and repugnancy.
t: Link GST to Article 246A.

x: All three are correct: atomic energy and mineral resources are Union subjects; public health and sanitation is a State subject; local government and Panchayati Raj are State subjects (Entry 5). So the answer is I, II and III.
t: Classify each subject; public health is a State subject.
s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Atomic Energy and Mineral Resources are Union List subjects.
II. Public Health and Sanitation is a State List subject.
III. Local Government and Panchayati Raj are State List subjects.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: Both are true: radio and television broadcasting is a Union List subject, while electricity is in the Concurrent List.
t: Remember electricity is shared (Concurrent).

x: Agriculture and agricultural education – State List; stock exchanges and futures markets – Union List; adulteration of foodstuffs and goods – Concurrent List; cyber law – a residuary subject under Article 248.
t: Place each subject in its List; anything in no List is residuary.

x: Trade and commerce within a State is State List Entry 26, subject to Concurrent List Entry 33. Inter-State trade is Union Entry 42, and Entry 5 is local government.
t: Separate intra-State (Entry 26) from inter-State (Entry 42) trade.

x: A is incorrect: public order stayed in the State List (Entry 1). The 42nd Amendment moved education, forests, weights and measures, protection of wild animals and birds, and administration of justice.
t: Recall the five shifted subjects; public order is not one.

x: Three: weights and measures, protection of wild animals and birds, and administration of justice were moved in 1976. Public health and sanitation remains a State subject.
t: Remove the subject that was not among the five shifted.

x: Article 249 – Rajya Sabha resolution in national interest; Article 250 – National Emergency; Article 252 – request of two or more State Legislatures; Article 356 – President's Rule.
t: Match each Article to its trigger.

x: Three: agriculture (and agricultural education), land and land reforms, and fisheries and markets are State subjects. Radio and television broadcasting is a Union subject.
t: Remove the communication subject and count the rest.

x: The Code of Civil Procedure is a Concurrent List subject. Foreign affairs and treaties, census and corporation tax are all Union List subjects.
t: Procedural codes are Concurrent subjects.

x: Foreign affairs and treaties – Union List; tolls and capitation taxes – State List; Civil Procedure Code – Concurrent List; space research – a residuary subject under Article 248.
t: Place each subject in its List; anything in no List is residuary.
s:

List-I
(a) Foreign Affairs and Treaties
(b) Tolls and Capitation Taxes
(c) Civil Procedure Code
(d) Space research

List-II
(i) Union List

x: All four are Union List subjects: foreign affairs and treaties, banking and insurance, stock exchanges and futures markets, and inter-State migration and quarantine (Entry 81).
t: National and inter-State matters are Union subjects.

x: A is incorrect: public health and sanitation is a State List subject, not Concurrent. The others are right: tolls (State), inter-State migration and quarantine (Union), local government (State).
t: Check which List each subject truly belongs to.

x: Under Article 250, during a National Emergency, Parliament's laws on State subjects can extend to the whole or any part of India. 'Only consenting States' describes Article 252.
t: Distinguish Article 250's reach from Article 252's.

x: All three are correct: administration of justice was moved to the Concurrent List in 1976, covering all courts except the Supreme Court and High Courts, and Entry 20A (population control and family planning) was added.
t: Note the exception for the higher courts.

x: A is true: under Article 356 Parliament exercises the State Legislature's powers during President's Rule. B is false: Article 250 is triggered by a National Emergency; a request by two States is Article 252.
t: Match the trigger to the Article.

x: Under Article 249 the Rajya Sabha resolution needs two-thirds of the members present and voting — not two-thirds of total membership.
t: Distinguish 'present and voting' from 'total membership'.

x: Space research is a residuary subject (in no List); prisons are a State subject; defence is a Union subject; forests moved to the Concurrent List by the 42nd Amendment.
t: Place each subject in its List; anything in no List is residuary.
s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Space research
(b) Prisons
(c) Defence of India
(d) Forests

List-II
(i) Residuary subject
(ii) State List subject
(iii) Union List subject
(iv) Concurrent List subject

x: Both are true: census, including decennial enumeration, is a Union subject, and land assessment is a State subject.
t: Census is Union; land matters are State.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: Canada giving residuary powers to the Centre says nothing about why the USA and Australia give them to the States.
t: A fact about one country cannot explain another's.
